title: CEX Complete Guide
subtitle: Understanding Centralized Exchanges from Basics to Advanced Trading

intro.title: Introduction to Centralized Exchanges
intro.content:
Centralized Exchanges (CEX) are the primary gateways between traditional finance and the cryptocurrency world. Unlike decentralized exchanges (DEX) that operate entirely on-chain, CEXs function like traditional stock exchanges—with a central authority managing order books, custody, and trading infrastructure.

In this comprehensive guide, you'll learn how centralized exchanges work, how they differ from DEXs, what features they offer, and most importantly—how to use them safely. We'll cover everything from basic spot trading to advanced features like margin trading and API integration, along with critical lessons from major exchange failures like Mt. Gox and FTX.

cex_basics.title: CEX Basics
cex_basics.content: Understanding how centralized exchanges work is essential for anyone entering the crypto market. Despite the crypto industry's decentralization ethos, CEXs remain the most popular way to trade cryptocurrencies due to their liquidity, speed, and ease of use.

how_they_work.title: How Centralized Exchanges Work
how_they_work.content:
When you use a CEX, you're not trading directly on the blockchain. Instead:

  1. Deposit: You send crypto or fiat to the exchange
  2. Internal Ledger: The exchange credits your account in their internal database
  3. Trading: When you trade, the exchange updates balances in their database—no on-chain transactions occur
  4. Withdrawal: Only when you withdraw does an actual blockchain transaction happen

This architecture enables instant trades and high throughput, but means you're trusting the exchange to hold your funds securely and honor withdrawals.

Custody Model: CEXs use a combination of hot wallets (internet-connected for quick withdrawals) and cold wallets (offline storage for security). Major exchanges like Binance and Kraken typically keep 95%+ of funds in cold storage.

order_books.title: Understanding Order Books
order_books.content:
CEXs use order books to match buyers and sellers, just like traditional stock exchanges. An order book displays all buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) for a trading pair.

Order Book Structure:

  • Bid Side: Buy orders arranged from highest to lowest price
  • Ask Side: Sell orders arranged from lowest to highest price
  • Spread: The difference between the highest bid and lowest ask

Order Types:

  • Market Order: Executes immediately at the best available price (you're a "taker")
  • Limit Order: Only executes at your specified price or better (you're a "maker" if it doesn't immediately match)
  • Stop-Loss: Market order triggered when price hits your stop price
  • Stop-Limit: Limit order triggered when price hits your stop price

Example: If BTC/USDT shows a bid of $42,000 and ask of $42,010, the spread is $10. A market buy order would execute at $42,010 (you pay the asking price). A limit buy at $42,000 would add to the bid side and wait for a seller.

trading_fees.title: Trading Fees Explained
trading_fees.content:
CEX fees vary significantly between platforms and are typically structured as maker/taker fees:

Maker vs Taker:

  • Maker: You add liquidity by placing a limit order that doesn't immediately execute (typically 0.02-0.10% fee)
  • Taker: You remove liquidity by placing a market order or limit order that immediately matches (typically 0.04-0.15% fee)

Fee Comparison (approximate ranges):

  • Binance: 0.10% taker / 0.10% maker (0.075%/0.075% with BNB)
  • Coinbase Pro: 0.40% taker / 0.60% maker (decreases with volume)
  • Kraken: 0.26% taker / 0.16% maker
  • OKX: 0.08% taker / 0.08% maker

Fee Optimization:

  • Use limit orders instead of market orders when possible (lower fees)
  • Hold exchange native tokens (BNB on Binance, OKB on OKX) for fee discounts
  • Increase trading volume to access VIP tiers with lower fees

Hidden Costs: Watch for deposit/withdrawal fees, which can be significant. Some exchanges charge 0.0005 BTC (~$20 at $40k BTC) for Bitcoin withdrawals.

cex_vs_dex.title: CEX vs DEX: A Comprehensive Comparison
cex_vs_dex.content: Understanding the trade-offs between centralized and decentralized exchanges is crucial for developing an effective trading strategy. Many successful traders use both: CEX for high liquidity and advanced features, DEX for privacy and self-custody.

liquidity_speed.title: Liquidity and Trading Speed
liquidity_speed.content:
CEX Advantages:

  • Deep Liquidity: Major CEXs have billions in daily volume, enabling large trades with minimal slippage
  • Instant Execution: Off-chain matching means trades execute in milliseconds
  • Advanced Order Types: Stop-losses, trailing stops, OCO (one-cancels-other) orders
  • High Throughput: Can handle millions of orders per second

DEX Trade-offs:

  • Limited Liquidity: Even major DEX pairs often have 10-100x less liquidity than CEX
  • Blockchain Speed: Trades limited by block time (12s on Ethereum, faster on other chains)
  • Gas Costs: Each trade requires on-chain transaction fees

When to Use CEX: Large trades, frequent trading, margin/futures, trading during high volatility

When to Use DEX: Privacy needs, new token launches, smaller trades, when you want self-custody

custody.title: Custody and Control
custody.content:
This is the fundamental difference between CEX and DEX:

CEX (Custodial):

  • Exchange controls your private keys
  • You trust them to secure your funds and honor withdrawals
  • Faster trading, easier account recovery
  • Subject to exchange hacks, insolvency, or withdrawal restrictions
  • Must comply with KYC/AML regulations

DEX (Non-Custodial):

  • You control your private keys via your wallet
  • No trust required—smart contracts enforce trades
  • Complete privacy (no KYC)
  • Risk of losing private keys with no recovery option
  • Risk of smart contract vulnerabilities

The "Not Your Keys, Not Your Coins" Principle:

This crypto mantra highlights CEX risk: when an exchange controls your private keys, you're relying on their solvency and honesty. The FTX collapse in 2022 demonstrated this dramatically—users lost access to billions despite believing their funds were safe.

Best Practice: Use CEX for active trading, but withdraw to self-custody for long-term holdings. Many traders follow the rule: never keep more on an exchange than you're actively trading.

privacy_kyc.title: Privacy and KYC Requirements
privacy_kyc.content:
CEX Reality: Most regulated exchanges require extensive KYC (Know Your Customer):

  • Government-issued ID verification
  • Proof of address (utility bill, bank statement)
  • Selfie verification
  • Source of funds documentation (for large deposits)

This information is stored by the exchange and may be shared with government authorities. Some exchanges have experienced data breaches exposing customer KYC information.

Why KYC Exists:

  • Regulatory Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Counter-Terrorist Financing (CTF) laws
  • Tax Reporting: Exchanges in many jurisdictions must report user activity to tax authorities
  • Legitimacy: KYC helps exchanges operate legally and partner with banks

DEX Alternative: DEXs typically require no KYC—you connect your wallet and trade. Your privacy is limited only by blockchain transparency (which can be enhanced with privacy tools).

Hybrid Options: Some CEXs offer limited functionality without full KYC (typically small withdrawal limits). P2P platforms also enable fiat-to-crypto without centralized KYC.

choosing_exchange.title: Choosing the Right Exchange
choosing_exchange.content: With hundreds of CEXs available, choosing the right one is critical for both security and trading success. The "best" exchange depends on your location, trading style, and risk tolerance.

security_reputation.title: Security and Reputation
security_reputation.content:
This should be your top priority. History shows that even major exchanges can fail catastrophically.

Security Indicators:

  • Proof of Reserves: Does the exchange publicly prove they hold customer funds? (Kraken and others publish audited proof)
  • Insurance Fund: Some exchanges maintain insurance funds to cover losses (Binance SAFU fund)
  • Security Track Record: Has the exchange been hacked? How did they respond?
  • Cold Storage Percentage: What percentage of funds are in offline storage?
  • Regulatory Compliance: Is the exchange licensed and regulated? (Coinbase is publicly traded and heavily regulated)

Red Flags:

  • Anonymous team or unclear ownership
  • Unrealistic promotions or yields
  • Withdrawal issues or delays
  • Poor customer support reputation
  • No published proof of reserves

Established Exchanges with Strong Track Records:

  • Kraken: Founded 2011, never hacked, strong security culture
  • Coinbase: Publicly traded (COIN), heavily regulated, excellent security
  • Binance: Largest by volume, SAFU fund, but regulatory challenges in some regions

jurisdiction.title: Jurisdiction and Regulatory Considerations
jurisdiction.content:
Where an exchange is based affects what services they can offer you and what legal protections you have.

US Traders:

  • Must use US-compliant exchanges (Coinbase, Kraken, Gemini)
  • Binance.US offers limited features compared to global Binance
  • Many altcoins unavailable due to security law concerns

European Traders:

  • MiCA regulation standardizing rules across EU
  • Strong consumer protections
  • Access to most major exchanges

Asian Traders:

  • More options including derivatives and higher leverage
  • OKX, Bybit, HTX popular in Asia
  • Regulatory landscape varies widely by country

Important Considerations:

  • Fiat On/Off-Ramps: Can you deposit/withdraw in your local currency?
  • Banking Relationships: Can the exchange accept bank transfers from your country?
  • Legal Recourse: What happens if there's a dispute? Offshore exchanges offer limited legal protections

assets_features.title: Supported Assets and Features
assets_features.content:
Different exchanges excel in different areas:

Asset Selection:

  • Binance: 350+ cryptocurrencies, most altcoins available
  • Coinbase: ~250 assets, focus on vetted, compliant tokens
  • Kraken: ~200+ assets, strong fiat pairs
  • OKX: 300+ assets, strong DeFi token selection

Trading Features:

  • Spot Trading: All major exchanges
  • Margin Trading: Binance, OKX, Kraken (not available on Coinbase in most regions)
  • Futures/Derivatives: Binance (largest), OKX, Bybit (leverage up to 125x)
  • Staking/Earn: Most exchanges offer staking and lending products
  • API Trading: All major exchanges; quality varies

User Interface:

  • Beginners: Coinbase (simple), Binance Lite mode
  • Advanced: Binance, OKX (professional trading view)
  • API Traders: Binance (best documentation), Coinbase (reliable infrastructure)

security.title: Security Best Practices
security.content: Even on the most secure exchange, your account is only as secure as your practices. Follow these essential security measures to protect your funds.

two_factor_auth.title: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
two_factor_auth.content:
2FA is mandatory for any serious trader. It adds a second verification step beyond your password.

2FA Types:

  • Authenticator Apps (BEST): Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password
    ✅ Secure—codes generated locally on your device
    ✅ Works offline
    ✅ Phishing resistant
  • SMS (AVOID): Codes sent via text message
    ❌ Vulnerable to SIM swapping attacks
    ❌ Vulnerable to SS7 exploits
    ❌ Not recommended for high-value accounts
  • Hardware Keys (BEST): YubiKey, Titan Security Key
    ✅ Most secure option
    ✅ Phishing-proof
    ❌ Can be lost (keep backup!)

Setup Best Practices:

  1. Use authenticator app or hardware key, never SMS
  2. Save backup codes in a secure location (password manager or physical vault)
  3. Enable 2FA on both login and withdrawals
  4. Use different 2FA for email and exchange (attackers often target email first)

Warning: If you lose access to your 2FA device without backup codes, account recovery can take weeks and requires extensive identity verification.

withdrawal_whitelist.title: Withdrawal Address Whitelisting
withdrawal_whitelist.content:
Withdrawal whitelisting is an underused but powerful security feature offered by most exchanges.

How It Works:

  1. You specify a list of approved withdrawal addresses
  2. Any withdrawal to a non-whitelisted address is blocked
  3. Adding new addresses requires 2FA and often a 24-48 hour delay

Why This Matters:

If an attacker compromises your account (phishing, password leak, etc.), withdrawal whitelisting prevents them from stealing your funds—they can't add their address and withdraw before you notice.

Setup Example (Binance):

  1. Go to Security Settings → Address Management
  2. Enable "Withdrawal Whitelist"
  3. Add your trusted wallet addresses
  4. Now only these addresses can receive withdrawals

Best Practice: Enable this feature even if it seems inconvenient. The time delay when adding new addresses is a feature, not a bug—it gives you time to notice and stop unauthorized changes.

api_keys.title: API Key Security
api_keys.content:
If you use trading bots or API access, securing your API keys is critical.

Key Permissions: Only grant necessary permissions:

  • Read Only: View balances and orders (safe for tracking)
  • Trade: Place and cancel orders (required for bots)
  • Withdraw: ❌ Never enable unless absolutely necessary

API Security Best Practices:

  1. IP Whitelisting: Restrict API access to specific IP addresses
  2. Separate Keys: Use different keys for different purposes (one for trading bot, one for portfolio tracking)
  3. Regular Rotation: Change API keys periodically
  4. Secret Storage: Never commit API secrets to GitHub or share them
  5. Monitor Activity: Review API usage logs regularly

Warning: Leaked API keys with withdraw permissions can result in complete loss of funds. Store them like you would store your private keys—in encrypted password managers or environment variables, never in plain text.

cold_storage.title: Don't Keep Everything on an Exchange
cold_storage.content:
The safest crypto is crypto you control. Follow the "hot wallet vs cold storage" strategy:

Hot Wallet (Exchange):

  • Only keep funds you're actively trading
  • Convenient for quick access
  • Higher risk—subject to exchange hacks and insolvency

Cold Storage (Self-Custody):

  • Hardware wallet (Ledger, Trezor) or paper wallet
  • Completely offline—immune to remote hacks
  • For long-term holdings

Recommended Strategy:

  • 20% on exchange for active trading
  • 80% in cold storage for long-term holding
  • Withdraw to cold storage weekly or monthly

The FTX Lesson:

In November 2022, FTX was the world's second-largest exchange. Within days, it collapsed, and billions in customer funds were locked or lost. Users who kept funds on the exchange for convenience lost access indefinitely. Those who withdrew to self-custody were unaffected.

The rule: If you're not actively trading it, it shouldn't be on an exchange.

trading_features.title: CEX Trading Features
trading_features.content: Modern centralized exchanges offer far more than basic spot trading. Understanding these features can enhance your trading strategy—but also significantly increase risk if misused.

spot_trading.title: Spot Trading
spot_trading.content:
Spot trading is the simplest and safest way to trade crypto: you buy or sell assets for immediate delivery at current market prices.

How Spot Trading Works:

  1. You deposit funds (crypto or fiat)
  2. Place a buy or sell order
  3. If matched, the asset is immediately credited to your account
  4. You own the asset outright—no leverage, no liquidation risk

Order Types:

  • Market Order: Executes immediately at best available price
    ✅ Fast execution
    ❌ Price slippage on large orders
  • Limit Order: Only executes at your specified price or better
    ✅ Price control
    ❌ May not fill if price doesn't reach your limit
  • Stop-Loss: Becomes a market order when price hits your stop
    ✅ Limits losses on positions
    ❌ Can trigger on flash crashes

Best For: Long-term investing, beginners, anyone uncomfortable with leverage

margin_trading.title: Margin Trading
margin_trading.content:
Margin trading lets you borrow funds from the exchange to increase your position size, amplifying both gains and losses.

How Margin Trading Works:

  1. You deposit collateral (e.g., 1 BTC)
  2. Exchange lends you additional funds (e.g., 2 BTC at 3x leverage)
  3. You can now trade with 3 BTC total
  4. You pay hourly interest on borrowed funds
  5. If your position loses value and collateral drops below maintenance margin, you're liquidated

Leverage Levels:

  • 3x-5x: Conservative leverage, lower liquidation risk
  • 10x: High risk—10% adverse move = liquidation
  • 20x+: Extremely dangerous—5% move can liquidate you

Example Trade:

You have $10,000 and believe BTC will rise from $40,000 to $44,000 (10% gain).

  • Spot (no leverage): 10% price increase = $1,000 profit
  • 5x leverage: 10% price increase = $5,000 profit (50% return)
    BUT: 10% price decrease = -$5,000 (you'd need $15,000 collateral, so you'd be liquidated around -8%)

Risks:

  • Liquidation can happen during flash crashes, even if price recovers
  • Interest charges accumulate continuously
  • Emotions intensify—leverage makes panic selling more likely

Available On: Binance, OKX, Kraken, Bybit (not Coinbase in most regions)

futures_derivatives.title: Futures and Derivatives
futures_derivatives.content:
Futures let you bet on the future price of an asset without owning it. CEX futures are typically perpetual contracts—they don't expire.

Perpetual Futures Explained:

  • Trade BTC without actually holding BTC
  • Long (bet price goes up) or short (bet price goes down)
  • Leverage up to 125x on some exchanges
  • Funding rate mechanism keeps perpetual price close to spot price

Funding Rates:

Every 8 hours, traders pay/receive funding based on the difference between perpetual and spot prices:

  • Positive funding (perpetual > spot): Longs pay shorts
  • Negative funding (perpetual < spot): Shorts pay longs
  • Typically 0.01-0.1% every 8 hours (0.03-0.3% daily)

Why Trade Futures:

  • Short selling: Profit from price declines
  • Hedging: Protect spot holdings with short futures
  • Capital efficiency: No need to hold underlying asset
  • Tax optimization: Different tax treatment in some jurisdictions

Extreme Risk Warning:

High leverage futures are where most retail traders lose money. At 100x leverage, a 1% price move against you = 100% loss (liquidation). Many exchanges show that 70-80% of futures traders lose money.

Use Cases for Responsible Trading:

  • Hedging spot positions (not speculation)
  • Low leverage (3x-5x) with strict stop-losses
  • Short-term trades based on solid technical analysis

earn_products.title: Staking and Earn Products
earn_products.content:
Most CEXs offer yield products that let you earn passive income on idle crypto holdings.

Staking:

  • Earn rewards by participating in proof-of-stake networks
  • Typical yields: 3-15% APY depending on asset
  • May have lock-up periods (7-90 days)
  • Examples: ETH staking (3-4%), SOL (5-7%), DOT (10-15%)

Flexible Savings:

  • Lend your crypto to margin traders
  • No lock-up—withdraw anytime
  • Lower yields than locked staking (1-5% typical)

Fixed Savings:

  • Lock funds for fixed period (30/60/90 days)
  • Higher yields (5-10%+ on stablecoins)
  • Cannot withdraw early without penalties

DeFi Integrations:

Some exchanges offer DeFi yield products (Binance Liquid Swap, OKX Earn). These are often repackaged DeFi protocols—same risks as direct DeFi use plus exchange counterparty risk.

Risk Considerations:

  • You're lending to the exchange—subject to their solvency
  • Yields are not guaranteed—rates fluctuate
  • In exchange bankruptcy, earn products may be treated as unsecured loans
  • Tax implications vary by jurisdiction

Best Practice: Only stake amounts you're comfortable leaving on the exchange. For large holdings, consider running your own validator or using DeFi protocols directly.

risks.title: CEX Risks and Historical Failures
risks.content: The history of centralized exchanges is littered with spectacular failures. Understanding these cases isn't about fear-mongering—it's about learning from patterns and making informed decisions.

exchange_hacks.title: Exchange Hacks and Security Breaches
exchange_hacks.content:
Even the largest exchanges have been hacked. Here are the major incidents:

Major Exchange Hacks:

  • Coincheck (2018): $530M stolen—largest crypto hack at the time
  • Binance (2019): $40M stolen via phishing—covered by SAFU fund, users reimbursed
  • KuCoin (2020): $280M stolen—mostly recovered through blockchain tracking
  • Poly Network (2021): $600M stolen—hacker returned funds after community pressure

Common Attack Vectors:

  • Hot wallet compromises (private keys accessed)
  • Employee social engineering and insider threats
  • Smart contract vulnerabilities (for DEX-like features)
  • API exploits

How to Protect Yourself:

  • Choose exchanges with strong security track records
  • Use exchanges with insurance funds (Binance SAFU, Coinbase insurance)
  • Don't keep large amounts on any exchange
  • Monitor exchange news—withdraw if you see red flags

case_mtgox.title: Case Study: Mt. Gox (2014)
case_mtgox.description: Mt. Gox was once the world's largest Bitcoin exchange, handling 70% of all BTC transactions. In February 2014, it suddenly halted withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy, revealing that 850,000 BTC (~$450M at the time, worth $30B+ today) had been stolen over several years. The CEO claimed the theft was due to a transaction malleability bug, but evidence suggested mismanagement and possible insider theft. Users received only a fraction of their holdings back, and the bankruptcy case continues today. The Mt. Gox collapse was crypto's first major wake-up call about exchange custody risk.

counterparty_risk.title: Counterparty Risk and Insolvency
counterparty_risk.content:
Even without being hacked, exchanges can fail due to mismanagement, fraud, or market conditions.

How Exchanges Fail:

  • Fractional Reserve: Exchange lends out or invests customer deposits without disclosure
  • Commingling Funds: Mixing customer funds with company operational funds
  • Risky Investments: Using customer funds for speculative trading or loans
  • Bank Run: Mass withdrawals exceed available liquidity

Warning Signs:

  • Withdrawal delays or restrictions
  • Missing proof of reserves
  • Unrealistic yield offerings (Ponzi-like)
  • Regulatory issues or banking problems
  • Leadership changes or resignations
  • Aggressive expansion during bear markets

case_ftx.title: Case Study: FTX Collapse (2022)
case_ftx.description: FTX was the world's second-largest exchange with a $32B valuation in January 2022. In November 2022, it collapsed in less than a week. Investigation revealed that FTX had lent billions in customer funds to sister company Alameda Research for risky trades. When Alameda's positions failed, FTX couldn't honor withdrawals. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was arrested and charged with fraud. An estimated $8B+ in customer funds were lost or locked in bankruptcy. The FTX collapse was crypto's largest financial failure and demonstrated that even "reputable" exchanges with celebrity endorsements and major investor backing can be fraudulent. Key lesson: Proof of reserves and transparency aren't optional—they're essential.

regulatory_risk.title: Regulatory and Jurisdictional Risk
regulatory_risk.content:
Government regulations pose an often-overlooked risk to CEX users.

Types of Regulatory Risk:

  • Exchange Shutdown: Government bans or restricts exchange operations in certain regions
  • Asset Delisting: Exchanges forced to remove certain tokens due to security law concerns
  • Withdrawal Restrictions: Governments can require exchanges to freeze accounts
  • Tax Reporting: Exchanges required to report user activity to tax authorities
  • Capital Controls: Limits on fiat withdrawals or crypto withdrawals

Real Examples:

  • China (2017): Banned domestic exchanges—users had limited time to withdraw funds before closure
  • US (2023): SEC lawsuits against Binance and Coinbase over unregistered securities—could force delisting of many tokens
  • India (ongoing): Uncertain regulatory status—exchanges operate in gray area with risk of sudden changes

Mitigation Strategies:

  • Use exchanges licensed in your jurisdiction
  • Diversify across multiple exchanges and jurisdictions
  • Keep most funds in self-custody
  • Stay informed about regulatory developments
  • Have a backup plan (P2P platforms, DEXs) in case your primary exchange becomes unavailable

The Double-Edged Sword:

More regulation generally means more security and user protection—but also more surveillance, restrictions, and potential for government overreach. Choose your balance based on your priorities.

api_trading.title: API Trading
api_trading.content: All major exchanges offer APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) that let you trade programmatically. This enables algorithmic trading, portfolio management tools, and automated strategies.

getting_started.title: Getting Started with Exchange APIs
getting_started.content:
Exchange APIs typically come in two flavors:

REST API:

  • Standard HTTP requests for placing orders, checking balances, etc.
  • Request → Response model
  • Good for: Order placement, account management, historical data

WebSocket API:

  • Real-time streaming data (order book updates, trade executions)
  • Persistent connection
  • Good for: Market data, order book depth, real-time alerts

Setting Up API Access:

  1. Generate API key in exchange settings
  2. Set permissions (read, trade, never withdraw)
  3. Whitelist your IP address
  4. Store API secret securely (environment variable, not hardcoded)
  5. Test with small amounts first

Common Use Cases:

  • Portfolio Tracking: Aggregate balances across exchanges
  • Arbitrage Bots: Exploit price differences between exchanges
  • Market Making: Provide liquidity and earn spreads
  • Grid Trading: Automated buy low / sell high in ranges
  • Alert Systems: Get notified of price movements or order fills

API Quality Comparison:

  • Binance: Most comprehensive, excellent documentation, high rate limits
  • Coinbase: Very stable and reliable, lower rate limits
  • Kraken: Good documentation, decent rate limits
  • OKX: Comprehensive, good for derivatives

rate_limits.title: Understanding Rate Limits
rate_limits.content:
All exchanges impose rate limits to prevent API abuse. Exceeding these limits results in temporary bans.

Typical Rate Limit Types:

  • Request Weight: Different endpoints have different "weights" counting against your limit
  • Order Limits: Maximum orders per second/minute
  • IP Limits: Limits per IP address
  • UID Limits: Limits per user account

Binance Example:

  • 1200 weight per minute per IP
  • 50 orders per 10 seconds per account
  • 160,000 weight per day per account

Avoiding Rate Limit Issues:

  • Cache data locally rather than repeatedly requesting
  • Use WebSocket for real-time data instead of REST polling
  • Implement exponential backoff on retries
  • Batch operations when possible
  • Monitor your weight usage
  • Use multiple accounts or IPs for high-frequency strategies (check exchange ToS)

Rate Limit Response:

When you hit a rate limit, exchanges typically return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) with a Retry-After header. Respect this—continuing to spam requests can result in IP bans.

best_practices.title: API Trading Best Practices
best_practices.content:
Security:

  • Never enable withdraw permissions unless absolutely necessary
  • Use IP whitelisting on all API keys
  • Rotate API keys regularly (monthly or quarterly)
  • Use separate API keys for different purposes
  • Store secrets in environment variables or secret managers, never in code
  • Monitor API activity logs for unauthorized use

Error Handling:

  • Implement retry logic with exponential backoff
  • Handle network failures gracefully
  • Validate responses—don't assume success
  • Log all errors for debugging
  • Set up alerts for critical failures (order placement errors, connection loss)

Order Management:

  • Always check order status after placement
  • Use client order IDs to track your orders
  • Implement order timeouts—cancel stale orders
  • Set maximum order size limits in your code
  • Test all strategies on testnet or with minimal amounts first

Testing:

  • Use exchange testnet/sandbox if available
  • Start with read-only API keys for data collection
  • Test with small amounts before scaling up
  • Monitor trades manually for first few days
  • Keep detailed logs of all API interactions

Common Pitfalls:

  • Not handling rate limits → temporary ban
  • Hardcoded API secrets → leaked keys
  • No error handling → bot crashes at critical moment
  • Insufficient balance checks → rejected orders
  • Not accounting for fees → unprofitable trades
  • Timestamp synchronization issues → authentication failures

Recommended Libraries:

  • Python: ccxt (supports 100+ exchanges), python-binance
  • JavaScript: ccxt, node-binance-api
  • Go: go-binance

order_book.definition: A real-time list of buy and sell orders for a trading pair, organized by price level. Shows market depth and liquidity.

market_maker.definition: A trader or firm that provides liquidity by placing both buy and sell limit orders, profiting from the bid-ask spread.

taker_fee.definition: Fee charged when you place an order that immediately matches and executes against existing orders in the order book, removing liquidity.

maker_fee.definition: Fee charged when you place a limit order that doesn't immediately execute, adding liquidity to the order book. Usually lower than taker fees.

spread.definition: The difference between the highest bid (buy) price and the lowest ask (sell) price. Narrower spreads indicate better liquidity.

slippage.definition: The difference between expected trade price and actual execution price, especially on large market orders. Higher in low liquidity markets.

margin.definition: Borrowed funds used to increase position size. Margin trading amplifies both gains and losses and carries liquidation risk.

liquidation.definition: Forced closure of a leveraged position when collateral value drops below maintenance margin requirements. Prevents negative balances.

kyc.definition: Identity verification process required by regulated exchanges. Typically includes ID verification, proof of address, and sometimes source of funds.

aml.definition: Regulations requiring exchanges to monitor and report suspicious activity to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing.

cold_wallet.definition: Cryptocurrency storage that is completely offline and not connected to the internet. Most secure storage method, used by exchanges for majority of funds.

hot_wallet.definition: Internet-connected cryptocurrency wallet used by exchanges for quick withdrawals and operational needs. More convenient but less secure than cold storage.
